articles.text: Two Piedmont women in their 70s were attacked in separate incidents 11 minutes apart by a group of three male and two female juveniles on Saturday, May 6, at around 6:00 p.m. Both women were knocked to the ground then kicked and beaten by teens 14-18 years old who jumped out of a stolen 2019 black Hyundai Kona. The first victim was walking on Magnolia Avenue just before 6:00 p.m. in front of the high school, when four Black juveniles got out of the car, knocked her over and proceeded to kick and hit her on the ground for around five minutes. She suffered a broken pelvis and multiple contusions and bruises on her legs and arms. Piedmont police responded and she was taken to the hospital by Piedmont paramedics. Roughly 11 minutes later, another report was received by police dispatch of a similar attack – juveniles, both boys and girls, who got out of a black SUV and attacked a woman on El Cerrito Avenue who was in front of her house. The second victim said she was “struck in the head with a closed fist which caused her to fall to the sidewalk.” She suffered several injuries to the face and head and was taken by paramedics to a hospital. Both victims have been released and are back at home. The first victim on Magnolia is a retired Oakland and Berkeley school teacher. She also used to work at Juvenile Hall, so she considers herself knowledgeable about being aware of her surroundings. She considers herself lucky that her injuries were not worse. She gave the following account to the Post: “I was walking up Magnolia and I saw a black SUV pass me and park on the corner of Jerome facing the field. I didn’t think anything of it. Then I got to the middle school, the black SUV passed me again, and pulled over by the high school entrance. Four kids, piled out of the car and walked down as a group towards the middle school. I looked and I made good eye contact with them. And then there was a boy walking after them. He had a look on his face that I call a smirk, one of those ‘look out, I’m tough, I’m big.’ Except for the smirk on his face, he was a pretty nice looking kid,” she said. “Just as I passed him, I heard footsteps running up behind me. At the same moment, I felt my hair grabbed and then I guess they pushed me down. I don’t even remember. The next thing I know is I’m on the ground face down,” she continued. Her glasses fell from her face, cutting her nose, and then the group proceeded to kick her on the ground and hit her with something resembling a plastic bat. Although she covered her head with her arms, a barrette hair clip she wore was kicked hard enough to break. “They did kick me in the head obviously,” she said. “It did not appear to be a robbery. Their motive was to do harm and do some mischief and mayhem,” she said. The fact that the attack lasted minutes indicates that the primary objective of the juveniles was not monetary. “It seemed like hours while I was there, but probably was only maybe five minutes.” At the end of the attack the juveniles took her backpack. When they left, she took out her phone and called 911. The friend she was meeting at the Center for the Arts drove by, saw her and tended to her until the police arrived shortly after. While police and paramedics were attending to the woman in front of the high school, a call came in about boys and girls attacking a woman in front of her home on El Cerrito Avenue. The backpack of the woman on Magnolia was found by the police on El Cerrito Avenue and nothing had been taken. However, the victim on El Cerrito Avenue had her backpack containing an iphone stolen after being attacked. Images of the suspects and their vehicle were captured by surveillance cameras at the school. Detective John Lagios, in conjunction with other law enforcement agencies, was able to decipher the license plate of the vehicle. The car used in the attack was recovered in Oakland at 61st and Stanford Avenues in North Oakland, three days later. The suspects are described as three male and two female Black juveniles 14-18 years old, 5’4”- 5’5”, and 120-130 pounds. The police encourage residents to always be aware of their surroundings.

articles.text: Editor: I would like to express my opinion on healthy free school lunch. I believe that everyone should get healthy free school lunch for 3 reasons: it is easier for families, it has health benefits, and it provides social benefits. First: It is easier for families because it is not as much of a hassle for students to get out of their house for school. Students know they will get a quality lunch at school, and don’t have to worry about remembering their lunch box. Second. It is healthier for kids. Did you know that 1 in 5 Californians struggle with food insecurity? This means that they cannot afford clean and healthy food. If students don’t get clean and healthy food, they are at a higher risk of problems later in life, and not growing properly into adulthood. Third. There are social benefits. Kids get bullied for a lot of things, and one of those things could be the food they bring for lunch. If everyone gets the same lunch, this problem would not exist. Some kids bring homecooked food from different cultures and backgrounds. If we were to have healthy free school lunch, personally I would try to make what we eat diverse every day. Now that you know some of the health benefits, social benefits, and how healthy free school lunch is less work for families, I think it’s important that we make healthy free school lunches available everywhere and get the same benefits that we already have in Piedmont. articles.text: Editor I’ve spoken at the last two Piedmont Rec Committee meetings but want to add my voice once again to the desire to have permanent pickleball courts at Linda Beach. I know from attending the meetings that some residents have complained about noise but given that I live about as close as you can get, I can attest that you do hear the “pinging” of the ball – but I also hear birthday parties at the tot lot, bells and clamor at Beach School, softball, soccer, little league, men’s soccer games, lacrosse practice, ultimate frisbee, etc. at Beach Field. I can also hear the announcers calling football games at the High School a half mile away. I’ve lived here for more than 25 years. We bought the house fully aware that we were purchasing in an area ripe with kids and adults at play and at work. A community that came together to celebrate, to support one another, and forge new friendships. Those are all the aspects that pickleball provides the community. It’s truly one of the most welcoming to newcomers of any group I’ve been lucky to be a part of. The group has also been so sensitive to complaints…making sure to park their cars away from the school at pickup and drop-off times, to work to get quieter balls and paddles, and to put in hundreds of volunteer hours to teach the sport to kids and adults alike. Come out and try a game. You won’t be disappointed. –Amy Kaminer Chabot Space and Science McCutcheon Construction REVIEWERS Art Allyson Aleksey Anastasia Edel Dance Jaime Robles Film Chris Honoré Music Joseph Gold Paul Hertelendy Jaime Robles Pets Melanie Johnston Theater Robert Lee Hall Wine Reviews Bill McNabb ADVERTISING Nancy Kurkjian 510-626-2468 CIRCULATION Call 510-652-2051

articles.text: Editor: The trial at Linda Beach is demonstrating the importance and viability of dedicated pickleball courts there. Pickleball demand is surging, but prior to the trial, no courts were open in Piedmont for a majority of weekday hours. In the trial’s first stage approximately 60 players per day used the Linda Beach courts, a large majority Piedmont residents, and wait times were more reasonable. With limited court space in Piedmont, dedicating Linda Beach to pickleball is more than fair to tennis. The tennis courts at Linda are undersized and the least used in the city. Based on Rec. Dept. data, the number of pickleball players using Linda Beach is on par with the number of recreational tennis players using all of Piedmont’s remaining tennis courts, which occupy eight times the space. We are sensitive to neighbor concerns and are working to address them. Fears about parking have not materialized. The park area has always been vibrant, including an elementary school, dog park, sports teams, and buses passing on Linda Ave. and the bridge above. Prior to the trial, in four years of part-time pickleball play, the Rec. Dept. received no noise complaints, including when families were home during the pandemic. A survey found pickleball noise to be a non-issue. articles.text: The 29th annual Bay Area Bike to Work Day is Thursday, May 18. Join thousands across the Bay in biking to work, to school, to run errands, or wherever else. It is the largest bicycle commute celebration in the U.S. for more than 20 years. Its goal is to help bicyclists find new routes to work. With roughly half of Piedmont’s greenhouse gas emissions coming from transportation, more residents are switching to cleaner commute methods. A total of 57 Energizer Stations will be available on May 18 along bike routes in Alameda County. A Piedmont station will be located near City Hall at Highland and Vista Avenues, from 7 to 9 a.m. Stop by on your bike and receive a free Bike to Work tote bag. A map of the 57 stations is available on the Bike East Bay website at bikeeastbay.org/energizer. If planning to participate, you can take Bike East Bay’s online “Pledge to Ride” at bit. ly/42LyB8K to receive a map of energizer stations and recommended routes. For more details and to sign up as a volunteer, visit BikeEastBay. org/BTWD. For questions contact Piedmont Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman by email at adykman@piedmont. ca.gov.

articles.text: Police Chief City of Piedmont As I write this, communities throughout our country have been devastated by recent mass shootings. Just weeks ago, we experienced our own fear inducing event here in Piedmont when a student threatened to bring a firearm to school. The epidemic of gun violence is not limited to mass shootings. Thousands are killed by guns every year in suicides, domestic and crime-related shootings, and unintentional shootings. We know this is our reality. The Piedmont City Council and Piedmont Board of Education have both officially recognized the ongoing and exigent need to address gun violence. Meaningful legislative gun reform on a national level is beyond overdue. The current state of affairs leaves many feeling helpless, at a loss, and in fear. But we are not helpless. We can work to control what we have the power to control. As usual with our Piedmont community, concerned residents are taking the lead. Last year, two local representatives of Brady United Against Gun Violence approached former Superintendent Randy Booker and me about working together to address this crisis. As a result, we formed a team of PUSD administration and City staff who have been working with these individuals to identify tangible actions that could make our community safer from gun violence, again thinking about what is in our control. We identified several focus areas, starting with safe gun storage education. Often, individuals who own a gun assume their children aren’t aware and don’t even know where a gun is stored. This is a dangerous assumption. If you own a gun, always assume that your child is aware and take steps to ensure the gun is not accessible to them. Here are some actionable steps you can take now: 1) Always keep guns locked in a gun safe. 2) Use a trigger lock. If you don’t have one, come by the police department and we will give you one. 3) If you don’t want your gun, surrender it to us. We will destroy it free of charge. Juvenile Officer Hugo Diaz has begun this education work at a series of meetings with PHS and PMS Parent Clubs. We will be rolling out additional educational materials in the coming weeks on safe gun storage and other actions you can take, such as having the uncomfortable conversations about the presence of guns in homes where your child may be visiting. pages.text: Wednesday, May 17, 2023 3 OPINION From fear to action on gun violence By Jeremy Bowers Police Chief City of Piedmont As I write this, communities throughout our country have been devastated by recent mass shootings. Just weeks ago, we experienced our own fear inducing event here in Piedmont when a student threatened to bring a firearm to school. The epidemic of gun violence is not limited to mass shootings. Thousands are killed by guns every year in suicides, domestic and crime-related shootings, and unintentional shootings. We know this is our reality. The Piedmont City Council and Piedmont Board of Education have both officially recognized the ongoing and exigent need to address gun violence. Meaningful legislative gun reform on a national level is beyond overdue. The current state of affairs leaves many feeling helpless, at a loss, and in fear. But we are not helpless. We can work to control what we have the power to control. As usual with our Piedmont community, concerned residents are taking the lead. Last year, two local representatives of Brady United Against Gun Violence approached former Superintendent Randy Booker and me about working together to address this crisis. As a result, we formed a team of PUSD administration and City staff who have been working with these individuals to identify tangible actions that could make our community safer from gun violence, again thinking about what is in our control. We identified several focus areas, starting with safe gun storage education. Often, individuals who own a gun assume their children aren’t aware and don’t even know where a gun is stored. This is a dangerous assumption. If you own a gun, always assume that your child is aware and take steps to ensure the gun is not accessible to them. Here are some actionable steps you can take now: 1) Always keep guns locked in a gun safe. 2) Use a trigger lock. If you don’t have one, come by the police department and we will give you one. 3) If you don’t want your gun, surrender it to us. We will destroy it free of charge. Juvenile Officer Hugo Diaz has begun this education work at a series of meetings with PHS and PMS Parent Clubs. We will be rolling out additional educational materials in the coming weeks on safe gun storage and other actions you can take, such as having the uncomfortable conversations about the presence of guns in homes where your child may be visiting. When each of us takes steps within our power to improve the safety of our own lived situations, it improves all our safety collectively. Piedmont Police work daily to prevent gun violence – through proactive enforcement that takes guns off the street, through accepting and destroying unwanted firearms, and through other actions within our power as law enforcement. In the case of the recent threat to one of our Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers schools, the students who overheard a concerning comment did the right thing within their own power by telling their teacher. By the time you read this letter, we will have lost many more people to gun violence nationally. As grim as that feels, I know we can find power as a community, one household at a time, to make a difference by securing weapons within our own homes. Finally, we can and must reach out for help if there are safety concerns associated with the presence of firearms in a complex life situation. Piedmont Police are experienced with procuring gun violence restraining orders and may be able to remove the guns from the situation. articles.text: On Sunday, June 4, the Piedmont Community Church Chancel Choir will premiere The Image, a newly commissioned piece written by Minister of Music Stephen Main. Scored for choir, soloists and chamber orchestra, and with texts written by Dr. Main, this full-length cantata explores the theological concept of the Imago Dei, (the “Image of God”) in which humankind is made and the role it plays in Western history. With contrasting sections of dark imagery and shimmering ecstasy, this piece is meant to be thought-provoking as well as deeply inspiring. It will be performed one time at the 10 a.m. worship service. Essays written by Piedmont fifth graders Phoebe Kim, Susannah Cantrill, Eleanor Hathorn, and Levi Arbit won them top ten bragging rights in the Northern Californian region at the 21st Annual Celebrate America Creative Writing Contest on Wednesday, May 3, at the Chinese American Citizens Alliance in San Francisco. Phoebe Kim won first place for her essay in the “Celebrate America” essay writing competition sponsored by the American Immigration Council (AIC). Her essay was a poem based on an interview with her grandmother who immigrated from Korea. Kim has qualified for the national competition. As the young Piedmont scholars arrived with their proud parents, they were unaware of what they had accomplished until they opened their programs. “When I saw my face on the front page, I was very surprised, and kind of shocked. I didn’t know how to respond and then people were congratulating me all of a sudden,” said Kim. AIC started the contest in 1996; the prompts this year were “Why I’m Glad America Is a Nation of Immigrants” or “What Does It Mean to Be a Welcoming Nation.” At the ceremony the 10 regional finalists read their essays from the podium and received medals and trophies. Cantrill’s essay asked what it means to be a welcoming nation. Her submission asked readers to consider what impact even small choices have on an immigrant trying to find their footing in a foreign place. Arbit’s essay shared an account of his great-grandfather’s harrowing flight from Auschwitz and then his participation in the liberation of the prisoners. Hathorn submitted a poem that created a vivid picture of one immigrant’s journey as a microcosm of the many journeys that have created the United States. The judging panel included San Francisco County Supervisors Catherine Stefani, Aaron Peskin and Hillary Ronen, along with San Francisco Chronicle Education Reporter Nanette Asimov.

articles.text: A Piedmont family was recently featured on a reality show called The Parent Test. The show features the parenting styles of 12 different families across the country. I met up with six-year-old Juliette Leong along with her parents, Willa and Jonathan, and asked them what it was like to be on a reality show. “We were told they wanted to look at our parenting style because they want to see how a kid like Juliette was raised,” Johnathan said. “Then they went into what they consider a reality show environment.” Parent Test: Intensive Style The show wanted Jonathan and Willa to represent the “intensive” parenting style. But that did not sit well with them. “They tried to prove that we were abusive and all that kind of stuff.” “Yeah, they lied,” Juliette added. Willa, Juliette’s mother, was upset with how the show portrayed them. “So, the producer told us that you guys are the best parents ever. They said they came across Juliette’s YouTube channel and she’s so amazing we want to see how you parent her.” Piedmont Prodigy The Leongs said they knew Juliette was special from a very young age. “At around two years old,” her father told me, “people started commenting that she remembers everything and then somebody said we should have her tested.” At age four her parents decided to test her IQ and were blown away by the results. “[From] Periodic tables to all the Presidents, the Capitols… her memory’s amazing.” Six-year-old Juliette Leong practices the violin on her back deck. The Life of a Prodigy Juliette keeps her parents busy. With all her activities and ambitions, they are always on the road. They just got back from a trip to Carnegie Hall in New York City where Juliette performed. “She’s the youngest solo violinist to ever play at Carnegie Hall,” Jonathan said. “So, she basically runs us, right?” Willa added. “She wants to do so many things. When she was very, very young she told us she wants to sing. She wanted to sing the national anthem. And by three she was singing the national anthem.” Juliette wanted to perform on a very big stage. “So, we put a video online and then we did get contacted by Reno Aces and the Oakland A’s. She sang at the Coliseum,” said Willa. Pushing too Hard, or Hardly Pushing Some people have accused the couple of pushing Juliette too hard and that was how they were ultimately portrayed on the Parent Test. I asked them how they felt about this portrayal. “Oh, we said it’s quite the opposite.” Willa says they are barely scratching the surface of what Juliette tells them she wants to do. “So, she’s pushing us.” Because of her ability to memorize, she learns very fast, so Willa says she hardly schools. “I tell people that we maybe school an hour a day. Like it’s quite the opposite of what people think. She wakes up at ten in the morning, she eats breakfast, and we school until like noon and she has the rest of the day off.” “But we told them that. We said we’re free-ranging parents, but they said we’re intensive at least for that one hour we are home schooling Juliette. What’s next? I asked Juliette what her plans are for the future. “Doctor. Violinist. Artist. Pianist.” Ambitious goals. But if anyone can accomplish them, it’s this 6-year-old prodigy from Piedmont.
articles.title: The Reality of being on a Reality Show

They said they came across Juliette’s YouTube channel and she’s so amazing we want to see how you parent her.” Piedmont Prodigy The Leongs said they knew Juliette was special from a very young age. “At around two years old,” her father told me, “people started commenting that she remembers everything and then somebody said we should have her tested.” At age four her parents decided to test her IQ and were blown away by the results. “[From] Periodic tables to all the Presidents, the Capitols… her memory’s amazing.” Six-year-old Juliette Leong practices the violin on her back deck. The Life of a Prodigy Juliette keeps her parents busy. With all her activities and ambitions, they are always on the road. They just got back from a trip to Carnegie Hall in New York City where Juliette performed. “She’s the youngest solo violinist to ever play at Carnegie Hall,” Jonathan said. “So, she basically runs us, right?” Willa added. “She wants to do so many things. When she was very, very young she told us she wants to sing. She wanted to sing the national anthem. And by three she was singing the national anthem.” Juliette wanted to perform on a very big stage. “So, we put a video online and then we did get contacted by Reno Aces and the Oakland A’s. She sang at the Coliseum,” said Willa. Pushing too Hard, or Hardly Pushing Some people have accused the couple of pushing Juliette too hard and that was how they were ultimately portrayed on the Parent Test. I asked them how they felt about this portrayal. “Oh, we said it’s quite the opposite.” Willa says they are barely scratching the surface of what Juliette tells them she wants to do. “So, she’s pushing us.” Because of her ability to memorize, she learns very fast, so Willa says she hardly schools. “I tell people that we maybe school an hour a day. Like it’s quite the opposite of what people think. She wakes up at ten in the morning, she eats breakfast, and we school until like noon and she has the rest of the day off.” “But we told them that. We said we’re free-ranging parents, but they said we’re intensive at least for that one hour we are home schooling Juliette. What’s next? I asked Juliette what her plans are for the future. “Doctor. Violinist. Artist. Pianist.” Ambitious goals. But if anyone can accomplish them, it’s this 6-year-old prodigy from Piedmont. articles.text: Students and teachers displayed their talents at Piedmont High School’s talent show, “Phantasmagoria,” organized by the Piedmont High School Advanced Acting class and directed by senior Milani Juarbe. The show, filled with outstanding acts and memorable moments, was presented in the Alan Harvey Theater on Friday, May 12. With singing, dancing, and juggling, Phantasmagoria had it all. Audience members were humming along with one act and then jumping out of their seats laughing during the next. Competing acts were intertwined by skits performed by the Advanced Acting class, which added a theatrical touch to the standard talent show format. The skits poked fun at AP tests, sophomores and college essays. Acts included senior Kiralyn Ma, who showed off her dancing skills, freshmen Nate McKenzie and Theo Ferguson singing “Travel Song” from Shrek the Musical, and winners of the school’s World Language Classes Singing competition, Period 6 Spanish 4 Honors Class, with a prize-winning performance of “Ahora Te Puedes Marchar” by Luis Miguel. The Talent Show included students and teachers alike. Science teacher Andy Willats had audience members waving their arms to “Don’t think Twice” by Bob Dylan. Freshman Chaz AmitGuite, who showed off his amazing juggling skills, was briefly accompanied by acting teacher Kim Taylor. Math teachers Auben Willats and John Hayden got the audience to sing the quadratic formula to the tune, “Pop Goes the Weasel.” Three acts received awards presented by Spanish teacher Deysi Sahagen, P.E. teacher Jeff Peters, and Administrative Assistant Darlene Low. Sophomore Daneille Zaroukian’s stunning vocals in a performance of “Quiet” by Jonathan Reid Gealt won an award from the three judges. “The entire experience was so fun, I loved it. The whole production was really great, and all the other acts were really amazing,” Sophomore Daneille Zaroukian’s vocal performance of “Quiet” by Jonathan Reid Gealt won her an award from the three judges. The Advanced Acting Class organized a Talent Show at Piedmont High that included skits and performances. An act put on by one ofSpanish teacher Deysi Sahagen’s classes Senior Micheala Bini’s performance of “Candy” by Paolo Nutini received an award. said Zaroukian. “An added bonus was winning a catered lunch in the park. The whole show was just amazing and I loved performing in it.” The Advance Acting class awarded senior Micheala Bini, who performed “Candy” by Paolo Nutini, a fast pass at the upcoming “Day on the Green.” Bini’s act displayed her remarkable voice, and acoustic guitar skills. She was accompanied by English Teacher Eduardo Wolbert on electric guitar. “Mr. Wolbert keeps three guitars in his classroom, so at the very beginning of the year I asked if I could play the guitar with him and we just started jamming together,” said Bini. The audience awarded a $100 cash prize to senior Ben Kim, who astounded the audience with his violin. Juarbe found that directing a talent show is strenuous, but equally rewarding. “I was very happy with the show. Seeing it all come together with the lighting and sound was wonderful. I keep getting feedback from audience members saying that they loved it.” Senior Jonas Kra-Caskey at the front of the line of Spanish 3 students on stage. articles.text: An upset was nearly in the making in Mill Valley on Thursday, May 11 at Tamalpais High near the shores of Richardson Bay. But the Highlanders, seeded No. 3, couldn’t thwart the No. 1 Tamalpais Hawks in a sweat-inducing, heart bursting 9-8 loss in sudden death double-overtime. The loss came just two days after Piedmont upset No. 2 Acalanes 9-8, also in double-overtime. With a depleted roster, fatigue increased and Piedmont’s chances began to slip away. “It was a terrific game. We took Acalanes to double-overtime and were able to pull it off,” said coach Al Yu. “This game was a great one all around. The size of our squad and Tam’s was extremely different. To rely on the starters like we do, we have a lot of players who don’t come off the field.” “We went to double-overtime and really didn’t want to do that again. We don’t have a lot of players, so it’s hard to play back-toback long games like that. But it’s always fun to go to Golden Goal, when any shot you take might be the game-winner. These types of games are why you play. You can’t win ‘em all,” said senior leader Soren Dixon, who led Piedmont with four goals. Piedmont took a 5-2 lead by halftime, but the Hawks ate away at the lead to make it 7-5 starting the fourth quarter and eventually went ahead 8-7 with 9:22 remaining in the game. At that point some heroics were required from the Highlanders. “The best and worst part about it was the game was so close,” said Fredericks. I have friends on Acalanes and one of them was guarding me. When we went into the second overtime, I told him that I wouldn’t want this to go down any other way. We talked at practice how we didn’t want another game to go into overtime, Staff Photos Soren Dixon celebrates after scoring a goal in the first quarter. He finished with four goals against Tamalpais. Nate Fredericks scored three goals against Tamalpais.

articles.text: Taylor, Long place 1-2 in 800; Sorensen-Wald qualifies in 3 events In a highly successful North Coast Section Bayshore Championship meet for Piedmont’s track team on Saturday, May 13 at Hayward High. The Highlanders had 12 athletes qualify for the prestigious NCS Meet of Champions this Friday and Saturday, May 19-20 at Dublin High School. Senior Christian Taylor led the way, winning the 800 meters with a time of 1:56.27 in a field of 23 runners. Teammate and classmate Parker Long was second with a time of 1:57.42, one second back. Mateo Malko-Allen of St. Mary’s was first in the 800 but was disqualified. Spencer Sorensen-Wald (right), a junior, qualified for Meet of Champions in three events; the 100 meter hurdles, 300 hurdles, and pole vault. Jamie Schwarz (middle), a junior, placed fourth in the 800 and also helped the 4x400 relay team qualify for the Meet of Champions. Staff Photos Christian Taylor (middle, right), won the 800 meters at the League Champio0nship track meet and was 4th in the 1600. He qualified for the NCS Meet of Champions in both events plus the 4x400 relay. Earlier in the day, Taylor completed his primary event, the 1600 meters, placing fourth among 24 runners with a time of 4:20.77. He was 10 seconds behind the leader, Malko-Allen, but kept a strategic pace given that he would run in the 800 and 4x800 relay later in the day. Although he came away as the 800 winner, Taylor’s focus at the Meet of Champions will be the 1600 meters (the metric mile). “Today was my last 800, so I wanted to conserve a little bit in the 1600,” he said. “I was with the top boys through 800 meters and then they started to push the pace a little bit more, so I decided to pull back and conserve for the 800. I just wanted to qualify and I finished fourth, I’m hoping to take the 1600 to State.” “I feel like I’m in really good shape. This heat definitely takes a toll, but I know I’m in shape for some pretty crazy times. The heat just means I need to stay hydrated, I made sure to get a lot of water in and stay hydrated quite a bit today,” said Taylor. Piedmont’s mile relay team of Taylor, Long, Jack Zirkelbach-Ngai, and Sam Shelby finished second of 18 teams in the 4x400 with a time of 3:28.47, coming .43 behind Bishop O’Dowd. articles.text: Piedmont’s baseball team gets its Division 4 North Coast Section playoffs journey started today, May 17, as the No. 8 seeded school will host a game with No. 9 Branson at Humphries Diamond at 5:00 p.m. Piedmont enters the postseason tournament with a 12-10 overall record, though it didn’t qualify for the Western Alameda County Conference’s Foothill Division tournament with a 4-6 league record. Piedmont finished fifth in its first season since being promoted from the Shoreline Division after winning the 2022 banner. The Highlanders battled despite having just three seniors on the roster and a batch of players getting their first opportunity on the pitching mound. Branson carries a similar 12-11 record. Branson and Piedmont had just one common opponent this season, Justin-Siena, the No. 5 seed in the D4 NCS playoffs. The Highlanders defeated the Braves 12-8 in their second game of the year on March 2. Justin-Siena battled back to a 9-8 deficit after the bottom of the sixth, but Piedmont scored three times in the top of the seventh. Branson, however, succumbed to the 10-run rule to Justin-Siena early in its season as well on February 22. The Bulls trailed the Braves 5-4 following the first two innings and progressed the lead to 9-5 before adding six runs in the bottom of the sixth to activate the 10-run rule. Branson’s leading hitter is senior William Ashley, who is carrying a stellar .418 batting average with 33 hits, 29 RBIs, six doubles, two triples, and five home runs. Noam AuYeung, meanwhile, is hitting .370 with six triples, and Liam Parrot has five triples and a .353 average. Similar to Piedmont, the Bulls have used a mixed bag of pitchers so far this season with three players with over 10 appearances and two more with nine. The starting pitcher will likely be Wilson Wendt, who has accumulated 45 innings pitched, 34 strikeouts, and carry’s an ERA of 3.89. The Highlanders are led by Michael Aikawa, Ryan McConathy, Will Parker, Markos Lagios, Peter Krumins, and Dimitri Papahadjopoulos. Aikawa has committed to play college ball at Lewis & Clark college in Portland. He leads the team in hitting with a .368 batting average, 10 doubles, while his one home run Piedmont senior Michael Aikawa is the team’s leading hitter and leading pitcher going into the North Coast Section playoffs. Sophomore Markos Lagios carries a .303 batting average with nine doubles, three triples, two home runs, 18 RBIs, and 22 runs scored.

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ tennis team saw its season come to an end in the semifinals of the Division 2 North Coast Section Team Championship, losing to No. 1 ranked Branson 5-2 on Saturday, May 13 at the College of Marin in Kentfield. The Bulls went on to win the title over University. To reach the finals, Piedmont defeated No. 13 Justin-Siena 6-1 in the first round on Tuesday, May 9, and followed up with a 4-3 victory over Lick Wilmerding on Thursday, May 11. Both matches were played in Piedmont. “Branson was very strong from top to bottom and wound up winning the championship, defeating University 4-3,” explained PHS coach Jim Landes.”Corey [Reich] and I enjoyed coaching the boys this season. We played a lot of tennis, despite a lot of rain in March. articles.text: Piedmont Middle School’s ultimate frisbee team, Purple Reign, competed last weekend in the Spaghetti Western, a two-day youth ultimate tournament hosted by Bay Area Disc Association in Tracy. It is the largest and most competitive competition in the state, bringing teams from Napa, Sacramento, Santa Cruz, San Francisco, Alameda, Oakland, Berkeley, Mountain View, and even Mexico. Competing in Division 1 for the first time on Saturday, Piedmont played through intermittent rain and finished with an 0-2 record. Seeded No. 6 the team bounced back and won the 5th place bracket game against Baja Sunset 6-5, Purple Rain received exceptional zone defense play from Aidan Stewart, Drew DeVries, Noah Hildebrand, Ben McMurtry, Ari Lopez, Danilo Titterton and Matias Seelenberger. Purple Reign returned on Sunday to compete in Division 2. Wins over Alameda Taurus, 11-8, and Davis Sprockets,11-3, put Piedmont the team in the championship bracket. Am 11-3 semifinal win over the Stanley Middle School Wildcats advanced Purple Reign to the championship game with the Eagles from Mountain View. Solid play from 8th graders Leyton Poole and Ryan Wendel, along with stellar defense from 7th graders Ariel Grossberg and Shane McNulty, helped guide Purple Reign to the win. It is the first tournament win for a team on which no player has more than 1-1/2 seasons of playing experience. “We’re incredibly proud of our team,” said coach Carolyn Stewart. “There was gritty play all weekend and it was a full team effort. They supported one another no matter the score, and they earned this championship,” Photos by Cisco DeVries Danilo Titterton scoring the winning goal in the championship game versus the Eagles. articles.text: Photo by Chris Hardy Smuin artists Ricardo Dyer (left), Alison Ramoran, Brennan Wall, Marc LaPierre, and Mengjun Chen with the company in Amy Seiwert’s world premiere of French Kiss, unveiled in Smuin’s “Dance Series 2” touring the Bay Area through May 28. We stumble through life and taxes, and then we meet the compact Smuin Ballet which has emerged from the pandemic seemingly unscathed. Its newest Bay Area run showed off 17 beautifully coordinated and trained dancers in pieces new and old, bursting with precision and energy. Purists may carp about the troupe’s leanings toward the commercial, but this group under Celia Fushille offers both sides, serving up contemporary with a capital C, abetted by the new associate director and adroit choreographer Amy Seiwert. The engrossing opening-night program offered the wake-up call via a twin-barrel blast of culture: Val Caniparoli’s earth-shaking foray into a stormy percussive world, and Seiwert’s light-hearted world premiere to French songs so much in the spirit of founder Michael Smuin. (Smuin in early years had actually performed as a nightclub show duo with partner-spouse Paula Tracy – not exactly your typical dancer’s CV.) Seiwert’s piece “French Kiss” showed itself as airy as a sunny Sunday on the Champs-Élysées, with skirts in alluring sherbet-pastel colors, whirled about by cosmopolitan sophisticates. The dozen players flowed on and off stage as smooth as silk, mostly in pairs. No, no kisses, but a lot of youthful exuberance to French songs from the Pink Martini ensemble. Perhaps with a bow to Magritte, a group of dancers hit the stage flourishing black umbrellas, evolving into part of the whimsical décor. Another Seiwert-only touch was the mannequin pas de deux, so appropriate for these AI days, with life-size plastic figures wheeled around by flesh-andblood partners. This sure-fire crowd-pleaser capped the first night at the Lesher Center. And yet what bowled me most over was Caniparoli’s rugged ritual Swipe (2011), as jostling as driving with four flat tires. The bold shoulder swivel-thrusts and bobbing necks had me instinctively flexing muscles dormant for ages. The performers provocatively raised and worked hands on high – I couldn’t tell whether they were waving to Aunt Matilda in the 12th row or simply satirizing empty political speeches, which already anticipate 2024. The high point April 28 was a pairing of Cassidy Isaacson and João Sampaio, nimble and athletic to the core. Among Caniparoli’s quirky enigmas came a woman’s extended leg (Isaacson again) doing a breath-taking full-360 like a sweep-second hand of a clock, in a display of flexibility par excellence, one that’s very rarely done on stage. The program opened with Katarzyna Skarpetowska’s Sextette for four women and two men dancing to Bach, memorable for the skyward leaps of Ricardo Dyer, a dabbler in lofty elevation. In between, Smuin’s duet “Dream” was a vehicle for ballerina Tessa Barbour in a long voluptuous formal, later partnered by the Brazilian flash Sampaio. Of note in this program was the meticulous preparation of the ensemble, with letter-perfect formations, pliable bodies, and ballet moves to remember. Casts change nightly. All the music is prerecorded. Seiwert, just promoted to associate artistic director, turned up at intermission to meet patrons, along with Fushille, in a refreshing turnabout from those troupes that rarely show their directors offstage. SMUIN CONTEMPORARY BALLET opened its 29th season April 28-29 at Walnut Creek’s Lesher Center, then San Francisco’s Yerba Buena Center May 5-14, and Mountain View’s CPA May 25-28. Details online, www. smuinballet.org.
articles.title: Smuin Ballet thrives with choreography of Amy Seiwert

articles.text: American Conservatory Theatre (ACT) will produce Wizard of Oz from June 1-25 at the Toni Rembe Theatre in downtown San Francisco. The classic tale by L. Frank Baum is transformed for the ACT stage by Tony Award–nominated director and choreographer Sam Pinkleton and Tony Award-winning designer David Zinn. “The myth of Dorothy and her friends, and their big adventure, means something different to every single person you ask—whether it’s childhood nostalgia, queer survival, or an unhealthy obsession with flying monkeys,” said Pinkleton. “I’m giddy and honored to enlist the brains, heart, and courage of the Bay Area—in collaboration with mega-genius David Zinn—to create an intimate, intergenerational, human-powered Wizard of Oz that is bursting with contradictions and big beating hearts.” The play is family-friendly and appropriate for young audiences. The cast includes El Beh, Keiko Shimosato, Darryl Jones, Katrina McGraw, Kunal Prasad, Ezra Reaves, Cathleen Riddley and Travis Rowland. For more infor mation, and to purchase tickets, visit https://www.act-sf.org/whatson/202223-season/wizard-of-oz/. ACT will produce Wizard of Oz starting on June 1.

By Paul Hertelendy We stumble through life and taxes, and then we meet the compact Smuin Ballet which has emerged from the pandemic seemingly unscathed. Its newest Bay Area run showed off 17 beautifully coordinated and trained dancers in pieces new and old, bursting with precision and energy. Purists may carp about the troupe’s leanings toward the commercial, but this group under Celia Fushille offers both sides, serving up contemporary with a capital C, abetted by the new associate director and adroit choreographer Amy Seiwert. The engrossing opening-night program offered the wake-up call via a twin-barrel blast of culture: Val Caniparoli’s earth-shaking foray into a stormy percussive world, and Seiwert’s light-hearted world premiere to French songs so much in the spirit of founder Michael Smuin. (Smuin in early years had actually performed as a nightclub show duo with partner-spouse Paula Tracy – not exactly your typical dancer’s CV.) Seiwert’s piece “French Kiss” showed itself as airy as a sunny Sunday on the Champs-Élysées, with skirts in alluring sherbet-pastel colors, whirled about by cosmopolitan sophisticates. The dozen players flowed on and off stage as smooth as silk, mostly in pairs. No, no kisses, but a lot of youthful exuberance to French songs from the Pink Martini ensemble. Perhaps with a bow to Magritte, a group of dancers hit the stage flourishing black umbrellas, evolving into part of the whimsical décor. Another Seiwert-only touch was the mannequin pas de deux, so appropriate for these AI days, with life-size plastic figures wheeled around by flesh-andblood partners. This sure-fire crowd-pleaser capped the first night at the Lesher Center. And yet what bowled me most over was Caniparoli’s rugged ritual Swipe (2011), as jostling as driving with four flat tires. The bold shoulder swivel-thrusts and bobbing necks had me instinctively flexing muscles dormant for ages. The performers provocatively raised and worked hands on high – I couldn’t tell whether they were waving to Aunt Matilda in the 12th row or simply satirizing empty political speeches, which already anticipate 2024. The high point April 28 was a pairing of Cassidy Isaacson and João Sampaio, nimble and athletic to the core. Among Caniparoli’s quirky enigmas came a woman’s extended leg (Isaacson again) doing a breath-taking full-360 like a sweep-second hand of a clock, in a display of flexibility par excellence, one that’s very rarely done on stage. The program opened with Katarzyna Skarpetowska’s Sextette for four women and two men dancing to Bach, memorable for the skyward leaps of Ricardo Dyer, a dabbler in lofty elevation. In between, Smuin’s duet “Dream” was a vehicle for ballerina Tessa Barbour in a long voluptuous formal, later partnered by the Brazilian flash Sampaio. Of note in this program was the meticulous preparation of the ensemble, with letter-perfect formations, pliable bodies, and ballet moves to remember. Casts change nightly. All the music is prerecorded. Seiwert, just promoted to associate artistic director, turned up at intermission to meet patrons, along with Fushille, in a refreshing turnabout from those troupes that rarely show their directors offstage. SMUIN CONTEMPORARY BALLET opened its 29th season April 28-29 at Walnut Creek’s Lesher Center, then San Francisco’s Yerba Buena Center May 5-14, and Mountain View’s CPA May 25-28. articles.text: Review by Paul Hertelendy With his audacious programming, credit veteran Director Robert Geary for pushing his Volti Chamber Singers a hair beyond. While Volti is not the most accomplished of our many chamber choruses, it is arguably the most adventurous. In their current concert set of five a capella works, the oldest one was two years old. Many a chorus (perhaps like one you’ve been in) manages four-part harmony, perhaps with keyboard accompaniment. But here there are eight-part unaccompanied harmonies, along with precarious melismas, offbeat chords and chaos, shouts and stretches of one’s range. It’s like being parachuted into a trackless jungle with just hunting knives and matches. If there were common themes in the current concert lineup, they were the composers’ greater interest in the sounds than specific texts, as well as in immersive issues of our day, whether the environment or concern about warfare abroad. Among the five works came a world premiere by Mark Winges, a U.S. premiere by Zibuokle Martinaityte, a previous Volti commission from Eric Tuan, plus pieces by Trevor Weston and Pulitzer-Prize winner Caroline Shaw, who had achieved that distinction while still in graduate school. Winges and Ms. Martinaityte were both in attendance May 13 for post-concert commentary. using less comforting intervals like seconds. In Hermatite, the ever-inventive Ms. Shaw played with the letters of F, E, O, bringing to mind the chemical composition of hermatite. And then out of the blue she tosses in lines out of the Columbus-contemporary composer Josquin des Pres, “A Thousand Regrets,” to voice thoughts on climate policy and an absence thereof, emerging in a muddy French that made you wish that someone had given Josquin English lessons. In a similar environmental vein came Eric Tuan’s In the Rain Shadow with the excerpt “Creosote Fractal,” alluding to a plant in the Mohave said to be many millennia old. Trevor Weston’s Given Sound was full of melismas and small clumps of words, showing off Volti’s well-focused soprano section. In the end however, the San Francisco-based group Volti needs to tailor its repertoire to the talents of the singers at hand, otherwise it’s just firing off illshaped rockets that miss the stars. Volti’s latest set was at St. Paul’s Episcopal Church in Walnut Creek, an attractive, modern structure with a large parking lot nearby. articles.text: Berkeley Symphony will host its annual fundraising gala, Symphony Soirée, this Saturday, May 20 at 6 p.m. at the historic Claremont Hotel, 41 Tunnel Road. Guests will first enjoy a reception featuring the music of Berkeley High Jazz Band, hors d’oeuvres, drinks and a silent auction, before dinner by Claremont Hotel Executive Chef Joseph Paire. There will be a special featured performance by Jazz Mafia and Cosa Nostra Strings, followed by an exciting live action hosted by emcee Michael Tate. Proceeds from Symphony Soirée provide vital funding for Berkeley Symphony’s innovative performances and its award-winning Music in the Schools program. Tickets and sponsorships are available online at berkeleysymphony.org or by calling 510.841.2800. “This year’s gala celebrates Berkeley Symphony’s commitment to our long-standing legacy of innovation and inclusion in music, and to help provide a comprehensive music curriculum to Berkeley public elementary students,” said Executive Director Kate Kammeyer. “The Soirée brings together the best Berkeley has to offer, and will enable us to create unique and diverse live performances, while extending our reach to thousands of students each year with Music in the Schools”. “We are thrilled to welcome the community to an unforgettable evening that celebrates Berkeley Symphony’s integral role in the arts and culture of the Bay Area,” said Berkeley City councilmember Rigel Robinson, a Symphony Board Member and Event Chair. Auction items include private culinary experiences, sound healing, and more! Soirée attendees can participate in the live auction, which will feature experiences such as a North Bay “foodie outing” with Berkeley Symphony’s Education Director Ming Luke, a trip to New York City to see Music Director Joseph Young in a performance at Carnegie Hall, and an all-inclusive stay at a charming German country estate. Jazz Mafia will perform its distinctly Bay Area hybrid of musical mayhem, marching band madness, soulful singing, and soaring strings, with a foundation of futuristic beats. Co-founded by trombonist, bassist, composer, arranger, and producer Adam Theis in 2000, the Jazz Mafia collective includes an eclectic group of forward-thinking and accomplished players in Electro, Hip-Hop, World, Classical, and Jazz. Twenty years in the making, Jazz Mafia is a prolific staple of the quintessential San Francisco sound, uniting creative and accomplished Bay Area instrumentalists, vocalists, MCs, composers, and arrangers. An offshoot of the Jazz Mafia collective, Cosa Nostra Strings is a five-piece powerhouse crew that features conservatory-trained classical and jazz musicians who find a common language in their passion for the music that is found in-between the lines. A unique instrumentation of cello, viola, violin, trombone, bass, vocals and percussion provides the perfect vehicle to explore the edges of the perceived musical universe. About Berkeley Symphony Berkeley Symphony is unique among Bay Area and American orchestras for its commitment to innovation, community, and excellence. Founded in 1971 in the intellectual and artistic nexus of Berkeley, California, the Orchestra is committed to performing, premiering, and commissioning new music that reflects the culturally diverse people and the heady creative climate of its home city. In the 2019-2020 season, Berkeley Symphony entered a new era under the leadership of Joseph Young, the Orchestra’s fourth Music Director in its 50-year history, following a highly successful February 2019 debut that was acclaimed by critics and audiences alike. In addition to building on the Orchestra’s artistic innovation, creativity and adventurous programming, Maestro Young is committed to amplifying the voices of underrepresented composers and artists as well as continuing to tell diverse stories that reflect the local Berkeley community. Berkeley Symphony Gala will be held this Saturday at the Claremont Hotel. ®

articles.text: San Francisco’s Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) celebrates Black beauty and femininity with the exhibit Black Venus, on view now through August 20. The exhibit is curated by Aindrea Emelife and is a reflection of the legacy of Black Women in visual culture, from colonial-era caricatures to the reclamation of Black womanhood by 18 artists of numerous nationalities and ages. Artwork spans from 1793 to the present day. Featured artists include Alberta Whittle, Amber Pinkerton, Ayana V. Jackson, Carrie Mae Weems, Carla Williams, Coreen Simpson, Deana Lawson, Deborah Roberts, Frida Orupabo, Ming Smith, Kara Walker, Maud Sulter, Lorna Simpson, Renee Cox, Sadie Barnette, Shawanda Corbett, Tabita Rezaire, Taiye Idahor, Wangechi Mutu, Yetunde Olagbaju and Zanele Muholi. The museum advises visitors that some artwork contains sensitive and difficult imagery. The exhibition’s thematic foundation is the Hottentot Venus, a visual-culture archetype named for the assigned stage name of Saartje Baartman (born 1789 in South Africa), fetishised by Dutch colonizers and slave traders. To learn more and to purchase tickets to the museum, visit https://www.moadsf.org/exhibitions/black-venus. Museum visitors view an item in MoAD’s Black Venus exhibition. articles.text: Paula Robles and Laia Artigas star in Summer 1993. Summer 1993 is a quiet, poetic meditation on childhood, focused on a six-year-old girl named Frida (Laia Artigas). Her mother has recently died; her father is deceased as well. She is told by her extended family (grandparents and aunts) that she is to live with her uncle, Esteve (David Verdaquer), his wife, Marga (Bruna Cusi), and their 4-year-old daughter, Anna (Paula Robles). Home for this nuclear family is the Catalan countryside, a good distance from the city of Barcelona, which is the only place she has ever known. From the first frame, the camera is centered on Frida as she struggles to comprehend what is a dramatic change in her life, a circumstance layered with a sense of abandonment as well as confusion regarding what happened to her mother. She understands very little about the sudden changes in her life, overhearing only bits and pieces of adult conversation. The truth is only hinted at, and what is implicit is gradually made explicit – AIDs was involved. Her father is a vague memory but apparently his death is connected to the same illness. With a gentle touch, writer/ director Carla Simon creates what is an autobiographical narrative of a young girl who is coping not only with profound loss, but also with the difficult struggle to adapt to a new family. Although her uncle and aunt are related to Frida, they are, essentially, strangers; however, they are consistently kind as they attempt to make her feel at home. The bucolic setting, the stone house, surrounded by woods, with chickens and sheep as part of the landscape, all represent a change that she finds difficult to fully absorb. Simon offers up these summer days in 1993 as a series of vignettes. For Frida, they are days of bright sunlight and nights of deep, silent darkness, far from the sounds of the city. But then this new world mirrors the resilient silence that she uses as a way of defending against a world she initially feels is intrusive and bewildering. Gently, the camera captures her isolation, her soft rebellion, a rebellion that can seem passive-aggressive. And to her new family, she can seem even sinister. Unexpectedly, Anna has an accident when she breaks her arm. She is no longer a toddler but is still defenseless. She acts out, pushing back in her own way against not only Anna, but against her uncle and aunt. Summer 1993 is beautifully rendered. But it is also a film that requires patience as it slowly reveals its moments of painful insights. It is not a movie intended for children. What is so powerful about this story is its ability to hold a point of view that is solely Frida’s. Think of it. A film that is a character study of a young, still forming young girl who is confronted with a world in which those closest to her are gone, most especially her mother. It’s remarkable. I’m reminded of one moving scene in the film in which Frida, in the dead of night, wanders into the woods with a flashlight. She shines it up, into the treetops, and calls out for her mother. Of course, she hears only the whisper of the wind, which only compounds her sense of having been forsaken. Summer 1993 is simultaneously remote and involving. It is subtle and elusive, sometimes repetitive as the days merge, one to the next. But always it’s about Frida’s search for love and reassurance; these are emotions that make all the difference to a film that finds its very special sweet spot. Summer 1993. Foreign film. Subtitles-language Catalan-Spanish. Starring Leia Artigas, Paula Robles, Bruna Cusi. 1 hr., 36 min. Not rated. Released in 2018. Streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Apple tv.

articles.text: Megan Leavey is a sentimental and heartfelt story about the connection between a young Marine corporal (Kate Mara), and her combat dog, Rex. The year is 2003. The initial setting is upstate New York where we find Megan at loose ends, adrift, feeling her life lacks substance and purpose. She turns to the Marines, endures a demanding boot camp, and ends up, for disciplinary reasons, cleaning the cages of a group of specially trained, bomb-sniffing dogs destined for Iraq. She makes the decision that she, above all else, wants to be one of the handlers and begins the arduous journey of learning how to qualify for and then work with a temperamental German shepherd named Rex. Gradually, they form a bond that Megan nurtures, and eventually are shipped out to Iraq, assigned to Ramadi and Fallujah. They are sent on 100 missions searching for hidden ordinance and roadside I.E.D.s. Of course, there are harrowing battle scenes along the way until eventually Megan and Rex are both injured in an I.E.D. explosion. Megan is sent stateside to recuperate requiring that she and Rex be separated. The film feels genuine, the attachment developed between Megan and Rex profound. Their connection is made manifest by the leather leash that Megan is determined to never release. Their partnership is jeopardized and of course the audience yearns for a right ending. Director Cowperthwaite (Blackfish) doesn’t disappoint. But then the audience knows this going in. It’s the journey that is so interesting as both Rex and Megan suffer PTSD, only to deal with it fully the moment they are reunited. Act three is about the struggle they endure to find one another. Megan Leavey. Directed by Gabriela Cowperthwaite. Starring Kate Mara, Ramon Rodriquez and Brad Whitford. 1 hr., 56 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2017. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv. articles.text: The Secret of NIMH is a wonderful, compelling story, both whimsical and thrilling. Its handdrawn animation is extraordinary, rich in detail and color, and follows the tradition in which animals talk and reason. It was adapted from the 1971 children’s classic, Mrs. Frisby and the Rats of NIMH, written by Robert C. O’Brien. From the opening set up, the narrative is flooded with a sense of urgency that fully engages the audience. Mrs. Frisby (Elizabeth Harman), a widowed mouse, lives with her two children in a cinder block located in an open field on the Fitzgibbon farm. She learns that the field is soon to be plowed and she must move her family as quickly as possible to a safe place. But she is confronted with what seems an insurmountable problem: she discovers that her child Timothy is ill. She asks Mr. Ages (Arthur Mallet), a friend of her late husband, Jonathan, to see the small child. He tells Mrs. Frisby that Timothy is very sick with pneumonia, gives her some medicine, and adds that the child cannot be moved for at least three weeks. The following day she learns that Farmer Fitzgibbons is going to start plowing early. Suddenly, time is of the essence, and she realizes that help is needed. With her friend Jeremy (Dom DeLuise), a clumsy but comical crow, The Secret of NIMH is adapted from the children’s classic, Mrs. Frisby and the Rats of NIMH, by Robert C. O’Brien. she goes to consult the Great Owl (John Carradine) for advice. He wisely tells her to seek out the rats who live under a large rose bush near the Fitzgibbon farmhouse. It’s at this point that act two of The Secret of NIMH begins. Mrs. Frisby is increasingly frantic to find a way to move her home without risking the life of Timothy. She discovers, on her visit to the rose bush that the rats possess a superior intelligence and have created a community that is beyond anything she has ever seen: it’s a warren of sophisticated technology and they even have electricity, which they steal from the Fitzgibbon house. It’s there that she meets the leader of the rats, Nicodemus (Derek Jacobi). He agrees to help her and gives her an amulet that will help her when she needs it most. Thus begins the adventure of Mrs. Frisby in earnest and the secret of NIMH (the National Institute of Mental Health) is revealed. NIMH is simply great storytelling by a group of ex-pats from Disney who launched a new studio headed by Don Bluth, committed to sustaining animation as an art form and not one ruled by CGI. This feature film was their first effort, and it proved to be warm and filled with thrills. A caveat for parents is that though NIMH has a G rating, it can also be darkly intense. The Secret of NIMH. Animated fantasy – adventure. Directed by Don Bluth. With the voices of Elizabeth Harman, Derek Jacobi, and Dom DeLuise. 1 hr., 22 min. Rated G. Released in 1982. articles.text: The film Chemical Hearts is a sensitive high school melodrama, based on the popular 2016 novel of the same name by Krystal Sutherland. The narrative is told from the point of view of 17-year-old Henry Page, who is just beginning his senior year, and eager to be the school’s quarterly newspaper editor. In voiceover, the film opens with Henry explaining that he has always wanted to be writer, but understands that his life experience has thus far been narrow. He’s introverted, has never had a girl friend, has few friends, his only hobby, strangely, is Japanese Kintsuei (repairing broken vases), and admits that he is waiting, with some frustration, for something to happen which will provide him with something, anything to write about. On the first day of school, sitting in his journalism class, he is told by his teacher that he will co-edit the paper with a recent transfer student, Grace Town (Lili Reinhart), also a senior, who has a previous newspaper background, walks with a cane, and shows, at least initially, no interest in working with Henry or the paper. She’d rather spend her time reading Pablo Neruda. Grace is mysterious, remote, and the ever present cane a metaphor indicating some previous trauma. Though initially standoffish, even hostile, Grace and Henry begin to interact (causing Henry to frequently miss his school bus). And so their relationship grows, and gradually she begins to share small bits of herself. She takes Henry to her favorite spot, they walk often in a nearby park, and he yearns to know more about her, while she withholds parts of her past. Slowly, Henry comes to understand that Grace is haunted by grief and a series of catastrophes; her emotions hang by a thread. Nevertheless, he can feel himself falling in love with her, and she begins, however reluctantly, to reciprocate. Chemical Hearts captures the chaos and confusion of adolescence. In the words of the author, Krystal Sutherland, “You are never more alive than when you are a teenager. Writer/director Richard Tanne gets it just right. Chemical Hearts. Directed by Richard Tanne. Starring Lili Reinhart, Austin Abrams, Coral Pena. 1 hr., 35 min. Rated R. Released in 2020, Now Streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv. Lili Reinhart and Austin Abrams in Chemical Hearts

She asks Mr. Ages (Arthur Mallet), a friend of her late husband, Jonathan, to see the small child. He tells Mrs. Frisby that Timothy is very sick with pneumonia, gives her some medicine, and adds that the child cannot be moved for at least three weeks. articles.text: Who knew, when movie stars Tony Curtis and Janet Leigh married, that their daughter would go on to win an award that eluded both her parents: an acting Oscar – at age 64, no less. But that’s just what Jamie Lee Curtis did this year, for her performance in Everything Everywhere All at Once. Fortunately for Piedmont, this limber, wry, sassy actress visited us last week, in one of her best early roles: Wanda in the fizzy 1988 heist comedy, A Fish Called Wanda. The film was the fifth selection in Piedmont’s new, monthly Second Thursday Film Fest. Adding to its quality, the deft comic actor, Kevin Cline, stars as Curtis’s lover and co-conspirator, and the pair are abetted in the movie’s non-stop mischief by a pair of Monty Python alumni: John Cleese and Michael Palin. Written and directed by Cleese and Charles Crichton, Wanda earned three Oscars, including Best Supporting Actor for Kevin Cline. It got a 96% rating from Rotten Tomatoes and was named by the British Film Institute the 39th best all-time English film. The comedy is littered with lies, betrayals, seductions and mayhem, and rarely has rampant bad behavior been so funny. The machinations of the plot turn on a theft of diamonds. Each of the cast plots to lay hands on them exclusively. Along the way, dogs are assassinated, and the climax of the tale involves a steamroller and wet cement. Where does that titular fish come in? At one point the key to a deposit box containing the diamonds is hidden in a fish tank. In a post-showing discussion, most of the audience said they liked the movie. It contains some profanity and sexual references, but no one seemed to mind, nor was anyone concerned about Otto’s treatment of the stuttering Ken – people saw it as an artifact of its time. One person didn’t like the film’s type of humor, but one enthused that she loved it. Next month’s Second Thursday Film Fest, on June 8th, screens one of the best of MGM’s technicolor musicals: The Band Wagon, starring Fred Astaire and Cyd Charisse. The Film Fest takes place each month in the Piedmont Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue on the second Thursday of each month. Doors open at 10:15 a.m., with the showtime at 10:30. The event is free and open to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, though registration with the Rec Department can be done at https://bit.ly/3PJyxkP. Audiences are welcome to bring snacks or lunch.

articles.text: The Piedmont Garden Club (PGC) welcomed the public to a grand display of natural beauty May 2nd through May 4th at the Claremont Country Club. At least 450 visitors arrived to see what all the cork-popping was about. The Garden Club of America-sanctioned Flower Show gave floral designers, photographers, horticulturalists and gardeners of all skill levels a chance to compete for ribbons and honors. Flower Shows like this are put on by industrious garden clubs to help set standards for artistry in floral design, horticulture, conservation and photography, and to broaden the members’ and the public’s knowledge in these areas. Dedicated to long time Piedmont Garden Club members, Mary Wood and Jo Shuman, who both passed away last year, the PGC show brought out the creativity, artistry and talent of those who participated. Key words including “Splash,” Jean Jarvis, Kathryn Pritchett, and Mary Lou Righellis Patty Reed Julia Burke and husband Bruce “Dazzle,” “Pop,” “Chill,” and of course, “Cheers,” were used as guides to inspire participants to take their creativity to new and exciting heights. Entrants weren’t just Piedmont Garden Club members, but included competitors from other GCA clubs around the country. Floral Designers took on challenges, such as underwater design (“Splash”), some went contemporary (“Dazzle”), and miniatures, (“Pop”) and functional table designs were clever and surprising (“Cheers”). Among the top honorees were Sherri Dumke, for her distinctive floral design, and Patty Siskind and Nancy Cecconi for their imaginative “functional table” design. Horticulture classes asked for Cut Specimens (“Dazzle”) as well as container-grown plants that had been owned and tended by entrants for at least three months. articles.text: The Wednesday before Mother’s Day, May 10, flowers were on the minds of the walking on Wednesdays group. Their destination was an annual visit to the Morcom Rose Garden on the Oakland border at Jean Street near Grand Avenue. The group first paid a visit to the home of walker Sherry Jacobs who was a recent victim of a mugging and strong-arm burglary. articles.text: A resident reported a catalytic converter theft in progress on Park View and Palm Drive at 5:47 a.m. on Sunday morning, May 14. Officers responded immediately and found the suspect vehicle, a gray GMC, occupied by two suspects. Their vehicle fled police onto Winsor Avenue where it ends at a parking lot at the lower Wildwood School playground. The GMC rammed through two security gates surrounding the playground and drove onto Witter Field. Realizing they were in a dead-end, two subjects left the car and ran away. An officer engaged in a brief foot pursuit until the suspects disappeared into the wooded area close to the baseball field and Magnolia Avenue. A search of the GMC revealed two freshly cut catalytic converters, at least two reciprocating saws, several blades, and miscellaneous burglary tools. At least one cell phone belonging to one of the suspects was left inside the vehicle and collected as evidence. A short time later one male suspect was located and arrested by Piedmont police. Victor Rojo, 40, of Oakland, had outstanding warrants including for narcotics. He was arrested and taken to Santa Rita Jail.

This is especially true in countries where signs are in a different language, rules of the road are dissimilar, and where parking has its own mysterious regulations. The alternative is public transportation. In Portugal, as in the rest of Europe that I’ve experienced, public transportation is very different than what we are used to in the U.S. The well-used train, metro, bus, taxi, ride sharing and yes…walking routes are most often well thought out. They are interconnected and coordinated, reliable, affordable, safe, and convenient. Using these alternatives to me is easier and less stressful than driving. Utilizing public transportation combined with walking is also fun—an important part of the travel experience adventure.
